I'd say a better place to start would be to change the political system, so more votes actually count.

Strongly opposed.

I just started a thread with the reason why here. In a nutshell, refusing to vote is a message in and of itself. Mandatory voting is just a way to hide voter disenfranchisement. The most recent election had the lowest voter turnout since 1942, right when we happened to be smack dab in the middle of World War 2. That is a major message.

The best idea would be to reform our voting system. First past the post (where getting 10% of the vote means you get 100% of the representation if the #2 guy got 9%) is just broken and invariably leads to an unsatisfactory two party system. Think about it. Imagine we have 4 parties running with around 25% of the vote each. Suddenly two of them decide "Ya know, there's a pretty good chance neither of us end up with any representation. Why don't we put our differences aside and team up? At least that way we'll get some representation!" Of course the other two guys realize what's going on and do the exact same thing. It's why you have libertarians, neocons and religious extremists all clumped into the republican party together even though their views are in many cases completely contradictory. You're left in many cases actually voting with people you seriously disagree with just because you disagree with them less than you do the alternative. Something I'm sure people of any political leaning in the US have experienced.

Here's a list of all countries currently using first-past-the-post: Anguilla, Antigua and Barbuda, Azerbaijan, Bahamas, Bangladesh, Barbados, Belize, Bermuda, Botswana, Canada, Cook Islands, Dominica, Ethiopia, Gambia, Ghana, Grenada, India, Jamaica, Kenya, Liberia, Madagascar, Malawi, Malaysia, Maldives, Micronesia, Myanmar, Nigeria, Palau, Saint Kitts and Nevis, Saint Lucia, Saint Vincent and The Grenadines, Sierra Leone, Singapore, Solomon Islands, Swaziland, Tanzania, United Republic of Tonga, Trinidad and Tobago, Uganda, United Kingdom, United States, Virgin Islands British, Yemen, Zambia, Zimbabwe

Notice anybody missing? Like the vast majority of the developed world?

Another good idea would be to drop the fear mongering and actually open up voting via the internet. If you can safely and securely bank on the internet, which millions do every single day, then you can certainly safely and securely vote on the internet. And you'd actually have a system whereby people could even easily research who they're voting on instead of picking from a list of a half dozen names 30 times, or even worse doing like the vast majority of America does and picking a party, pressing "Go", getting your sticker, going home, grabbing some beer and watching the circus unfold on TV like the sporting event it's televised as all while clamoring for your team to win.

In a nutshell, refusing to vote is a message in and of itself.

It's a message to politicians that they need to court an even smaller minority of people with strongly-held views in order to win. Politicians don't look at who didn't turn out to decide their message, they look at who turned out to find out how they can get those people to vote for them next time. Going to vote and voting for yourself or a third-party is a far more powerful message, because it will change the demographics a politician looks at when they decide what to run on. They don't factor in the people that didn't vote when they decide their platform, so turn-out rates mean nothing to them. By not voting, you're allowing politicians to safely ignore you, giving you less representation.

That said, I agree we need to move past first-past-the-post, and would be interested in seeing Internet voting.

I wouldn't hop on the net neutrality cheering bandwagon yet. The FCC seems to have intentionally set themselves up for a showdown, at least assuming they plan to enforce their rules. It all hinges on three words: "reasonable network management." The only thing that's strong about the net neutrality rules is paid prioritization - that is strictly prohibited, but everything else (for instance throttling, capping and blocking) is spoken against but always with an exception for "reasonable network management." That term actually appears more than 70 times in the rules.

Here's their only definition of it:

(f) Reasonable network management. A network management practice is a practice that has a primarily technical network management justification, but does not include other business practices. A network management practice is reasonable if it is primarily used for and tailored to achieving a legitimate network management purpose, taking into account the particular network architecture and technology of the broadband Internet access service.

Note the intentionally usage of weakening phrases like primarily technical, allowing room for throttling/capping/blocking for economic reasons so long as the companies doing so can come up with a "primarily" technical reason on top of it. The FCC themselves realizes how weak and ambiguous this is and came up with the decision of dealing with it on a case by case basis:

562 We recognize the need to ensure that the reasonable network management exception will not be used to circumvent the open Internet rules while still allowing broadband providers flexibility to experiment and innovate as they reasonably manage their networks.

563 We therefore elect to maintain a case-by-case approach. The caseby-case review also allows sufficient flexibility to address mobile-specific management practices because, by the terms of our rule, a determination of whether a network management practice is reasonable takes into account the particular network architecture and technology. We also note that our transparency rule requires disclosures that provide an important mechanism for monitoring whether providers are inappropriately exploiting the exception for reasonable network management

I can't even fathom how this is going to play out but I think you're jumping the gun a bit. Lifelong loyalties don't tend to just disappear because internet outrage, even if it was an unprecedented amount of outrage.

That's not to say NN as a topic is anywhere close to case-closed, or that there aren't many of battles left - or that it will ever be case-closed. But that decision was anti-industry practices no matter what way you slice it.

As for the reasonable network management clause, to be honest, I can't see a way you could create these rules without it. No set of rules can encompass the set of all possible cases, so saying as much is not unreasonable to me. Saying they're aware of possible abuse and will be watching for it is as much as you can expect from a governing body's set of rules; when it comes to actually putting that oversight into effect, we can only cross that bridge when we get there.

At the end if the day, it's a big first step that contradicts the actions of what you'd expect from a life-long lobbyist, and puts the government in a better place for oversight.

*33. Recently, significant concern has arisen when mobile providers’ have attempted to justify certain practices as reasonable network management practices, such as applying speed reductions to customers using “unlimited data plans” in ways that effectively force them to switch to price plans with less generous data allowances. They're clearly implying that that is not reasonable network management and even allude to Verizon implicitly acknowledging it wasn't reasonable network management, but they never come out strongly against it. At the most basic level, I can't see any reason that they could not have strongly specified for instance that a plan can not be described or otherwise implied to be unlimited unless it is actually unlimited as commonly understood which is to say unlimited access to unlimited data with untiered speed.

To the contrary, the new NN rules put in place ban not only paid prioritization, but any network meddling for business practices. A person engaged in the provision of broadband Internet access service, insofar as such person is so engaged, shall not impair or degrade lawful Internet traffic on the basis of Internet content, application, or service, or use of a non-harmful device, subject to reasonable network management.

This includes practices ISPs are provably currently engaging in. One example is the slowing of Netflix Comcast was performing since Netflix competes with their On-Demand service - to be clear, that data is showing Comcast slowing down Netlfix and not their own traffic. This is not the other issue Comcast claimed, which was that L3's connection with Comcast was being flooded, and which was why Netflix later paid to put servers directly into Comcast's data centers. By slowing down the connection for something that is not reasonable network management, that behavior falls under these new NN rules.

There's a lot more that should be done to the US voting system before they even think about mandatory voting. Since the president used Australia as an example of mandatory voting, here's what else they do that works well:

  • Preferential voting: There are many, many parties (although only 3 'main' ones), and you can vote for them all in whatever order you want. So if you vote 1 on someone, but they don't have a chance of winning, your vote will go to the person you voted 2 on. If they don't have a chance, it falls to who you voted 3 on.. and so on. You can also just vote for a single party ('above the line'), and the party makes deals with other parties in what order they will be if people vote this way. While this does lead to a few parties getting the majority of the votes, it gives third parties a better shot of getting a single representative into the government. Hopefully it can grow from there for them.
  • Voting is open for weeks - weekdays, weekends, everyone can postal vote. It actually allows people to get their vote counted without having to take time off work or whatever. The US system for this is fucking stupid.

Fix those, and then maybe think about mandatory voting. Mandatory voting in the current system is a horrible idea.
